slides.say: n is an integer. The expression n minus n cubed, over three, is always:

So n can be any integer. We subtract n cubed from n, then divide that whole answer by three. What is always true about the result? [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, plugging in numbers, and then writing the top as a multiplication.
[short pause] Let's start by plugging in. n is one would give zero. Zero is even and divisible by four, so those two choices would still both fit. Let's try the next small integer instead.
Use n is two. Two cubed is eight, so the top is two minus eight, which is negative six. Negative six over three is negative two. Now check the choices with that result.
Negative two is not divisible by four, so choice number one is out. It is an integer, not a non-integer fraction, so choice number two is out. And it is even, not odd, so choice number four is out.
Only choice number three remains, even. That is our answer, and we can stop. There is no need to try n is three or n is four. We have ruled out all three other choices with one allowed example.

[pause] Another way is to rewrite the top as a multiplication. n minus n cubed is the negative of the whole bracket, n cubed minus n. And n cubed minus n is n minus one, times n, times n plus one. Those are three numbers in a row.

The product of three numbers in a row always divides by six. The minus sign in front does not change that. So the top is a multiple of six. Dividing that by three gives a multiple of two, which is always even. Choice number three is our answer. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
